Special Protection Areas are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew

An investigation has found the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs is failing to protect wild birds.

The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas (SPAs).

The minister said it was "uncomfortable reading".

SPAs are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew and whooper swan, which continue to decline in Northern Ireland.

The OEP said action had not been taken to maintain or restore wild bird populations and their habitats.

The director of RSPB NI, Joanne Sherwood, said the findings were "no surprise" and called for urgent action.

The ongoing investigation began in 2024.

A parallel investigation is looking at the same issues involving Defra and Natural England, and they have also been issued with decision notices.

In Northern Ireland, the OEP's Chief Regulatory Officer Helen Venn acknowledged that "positive steps" had been taken, but added that delays in meeting legal obligations had played a part in the significant decline of wild birds in Northern Ireland.

"SPAs are important for achieving the Executive's commitments in relation to nature, such as the strategic outcome of thriving, resilient and connected nature and wildlife in the Environmental Improvement Plan.

"This is in addition to the Executive's international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature's recovery by 2030.

"This is why it is important for Daera to carry out its legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land."

The agriculture and environment minister Andrew Muir said there was "a moral and legal obligation" to protect wild bird habitats and welcomed continuing engagement between his officials and the OEP.

"The OEP has recognised in their investigation longstanding and concerning failures to implement recommended actions to protect wild bird habitats and populations by successive administrations both in England and Northern Ireland.

"While we have a long way to go to reverse current trends, there are signs of hope and clear examples of nature recovery in action.

"However, the scale of challenge requires greater levels of support from across government to provide the necessary resources and funding to address the nature crisis."

And he said the recently-published Nature Recovery Strategy and the Farming With Nature support package "reinforces" the department's commitment to nature restoration.

Sherwood said the group had been highlighting failing for decades.

"Today's findings from the OEP confirm what conservation organisations have been saying: action has been delayed for far too long.

"The focus must now move to delivery, with the Executive leading the way, and Daera and NIEA being resourced to take urgent action to put these protections in place and help reverse the decline of our most vulnerable bird populations.

"We hope today's OEP report will be the catalyst needed."

The decision notice is the latest step in the OEP's investigation.

It identifies failures and recommends what actions Daera should now take to fix them.

It says Daera has failed to classify and update SPAs, has not put measures in place to protect declining birds, and has not carried out a required review of habitats.

Recommendations include addressing outstanding recommendations "where they remain ecologically relevant" from a review of SPAs, carried out in Northern Ireland in 2001.

Where they cannot be implemented, it says "transparent, ornithological reasons" must be published.

Daera is also advised to identify the causes of declines and put in place resourced plans and effective measures to maintain or restore wild bird populations and the habitats they depend on.

And it says "the overdue habitat sufficiency review" must be carried out "as soon as practicably possible", to identify gaps in habitat provision and the action needed to address them.

Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell has criticised media organisations for broadcasting a message from the wife of jailed rapist Russell Brand on his behalf.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence .

The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.

"I was appalled at that [message] and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either," she told LBC on Wednesday.

"It's a platform I don't think should have been amplified, to be honest."

Powell went on to describe Russell Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

She continued: "This is somebody who's been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape."

In a statement, the BBC said the Today programme had played the Laura Brand clip "in error, due to miscommunication within the team", and had since removed it from catch-up service BBC Sounds.

BBC News has asked the other outlets named above for a comment, as well as YouTube's parent company Google about its policy.

In 2023, after a media investigation revealing allegations about Brand, YouTube suspended his channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy". But they are still available to view.

Brand's social media accounts on Meta platforms - which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

Earlier this week, Downing Street officials described Brand's message to his followers as "clearly appalling", adding that it was being urgently investigated,

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Sosiyete y’indege ya Uganda Airlines yatangije ku mugaragaro ingendo z’indege za buri munsi zihuza Entebbe muri Uganda na Kigali mu Rwanda, mu rwego rwo koroshya ingendo no kurushaho guteza imbere ubuhahirane hagati y’ibihugu byombi.

Izi ngendo zatangijwe kuri uy wa Gatatu, tariki ya 18 Ugushyingo 2026, zikaba ziyongereye ku zindi iyi sosiyete isanzwe ikorera mu Karere no hanze yako.

Ubuyobozi bwa Uganda Airlines bwavuze ko izi ngendo za buri munsi zizaha abagenzi amahitamo menshi n’ubwisanzure mu gutegura ingendo zabo hagati y’u Rwanda na Uganda.

Bwagaragaje kandi ko ibihugu byombi bisanzwe bifitanye umubano ushingiye ku mateka, umuco n’imibanire y’abaturage, ndetse bikaba bisanzwe bifatanya mu bukerarugendo, ubucuruzi n’ibindi bikorwa by’iterambere.

Iyi nzira nshya kandi izafasha korohereza abantu bakora ingendo z’akazi, ba mukerarugendo, abayobozi, abitabira inama n’abajya gusura imiryango n’inshuti.

Umuyobozi Mukuru wa Uganda Airlines, Girma Wake, yavuze ko gutangiza uru rugendo byari bimaze igihe byifuzwa, bitewe n’umubano ukomeye ibihugu byombi bifitanye mu bukungu, imibereho n’umuco.

Yasobanuye ko guhuza Kigali na Entebbe bizafasha kurushaho kunoza imikoranire hagati y’ibihugu byombi, ndetse bikorohereze abagenzi gukomeza ingendo zabo berekeza mu bindi bice bya Afurika, Uburasirazuba bwo Hagati, Aziya n’u Burayi.

Girma Wake yongeyeho ko uru rugendo ruzafasha kwagura amahirwe y’ubucuruzi, ishoramari n’ubukerarugendo hagati y’u Rwanda na Uganda.

Kuri ubu, Uganda Airlines imaze kugera ku Mijyi 18 ikoreramo ingendo zayo, aho Kigali yiyongereye ku masoko yayo nyuma y’uko ku wa 27 Ukwakira 2026 yatangije ingendo zijya i Accra muri Ghana.

Uganda Airlines ni sosiyete y’indege y’igihugu cya Uganda, yatangiye ibikorwa by’ubwikorezi bwo mu kirere muri Kanama 2019. Iyi sosiyete ikomeje kwagura inzira zayo hagamijwe koroshya ubuhahirane no guteza imbere ubukungu n’ubukerarugendo bw’Igihugu.

Abantu bafite ubumuga barasaba ko hashyirwaho umubare wihariye w’imyanya y’akazi igenerwa iki cyiciro, kugira ngo barusheho kubona amahirwe angana n’ay’abandi ku isoko ry’umurimo.

Iki cyifuzo gishingiye ku kuba bamwe mu bafite ubumuga bagihura n’imbogamizi zitandukanye mu gushaka akazi, zirimo kutagerwaho n’amahirwe amwe n’ay’abandi, ibikorwa remezo bitaborohereza kugeramo ndetse n’imyumvire ituma ubushobozi bwabo budahabwa agaciro uko bikwiye.

Gushyiraho imyanya yihariye yagenerwa abafite ubumuga ngo byabafasha kugabanya ibyo bibazo, bikabaha amahirwe yo gukoresha ubumenyi n’ubushobozi bafite, aho gukomeza gusigara inyuma mu gihe abandi babona akazi.

François Xavier Karangwa, ni umukozi w’Ihuriro ry’Imiryango y’abantu bafite ubumuga (UPHRS), avuga ko hari inzego by’umwihariko mu bigo by’abikorera zigiheza abantu bafite ubumuga, kuko udashobora kubona umuntu ufite ubumuga bw’ingingo cyangwa kutabona muri Banki kuri gishe (Guichet).

Ati “Urwego rw’abikorera uyu munsi ruracyafite akantu k’ihezwa n’akato ku buryo bidatanga umusaruro nkuko tubyifuza. Kuba bikimeza bityo bituma batagendera ku ntambwe imwe kuko ubundi mu bihugu byateye imbere, bafasha umuntu ufite ubumuga kubona akazi mbere y’abandi, bagashyiraho umubare wihariye w’abafite ubumuga mu myanya y’akazi. Mu Rwanda ibyo ntibirahagera, nibyo turimo dukorera ubuvugizi.”

Ati “Abagore bafite ubumuga ntibaramenya ko ayo mahirwe ahari, ntibarasobanukirwa uburenganzira bwabo. Ikindi n’abateye intambwe kugira ngo bahabwe akazi, abakoresha bamwe na bamwe, baracyafite ya myumvire yo kubonera umugore ufite ubumuga muri za ntege nke zo kuba ari umugore, afite ubumuga bikaba byatuma atabasha kugera kuri ayo mahirwe.”

Umunyamabanga Uhoraho muri Minisiteri y’Ubutegetsi bw’Igihugu, Bob Gakire, avuga ko hari uburyo bw’ikoranabuhanga Leta yubatse (Disability management information System), bukurikiranirwamo abafite ubumuga bakeneye ubufasha buri mu byiciro bitandukanye.

Ati “Icyo ni ikintu Leta yubatse kugira ngo uwashaka wese gufasha abafite ubumuga yababona mu buryo bworoshye, budashingiye ku marangamutima. Ibindi ni ugukomeza kubashakira akazi ku bashoboye gukora, ndetse n’abadashoboye gukora kubera wenda ubumuga bafite, abakuze tubaha imfashanyo igenerwa abafite ubumuga bageze mu zabukuru badashoboye gukora. Ariko icy’ingenzi ni uko abashoboye gukora hari gahunda tubazirikana yo kubashakira akazi n’abandi bose batagafite.”

Gushyiraho umubare wihariye w’imyanya y’akazi yagenerwa abafite ubumuga byaba imwe mu ngamba zo kwimakaza ihame ry'uburinganire mu mahirwe y’akazi, no kubafasha kugira uruhare rufatika mu iterambere ry’igihugu.

Ku rundi ruhande ariko, mu gihe mu Rwanda no ku Isi bitegura kwizihiza umunsi mpuzamahanga wahariwe abafite ubumuga uba buri ku wa 3 Ukuboza, abo mu Rwanda bishimira ko mu myaka 20 bamaze bawizihiza, hari aho bavuye naho bamaze kugera, kuko hari politike n’amategeko by’igihugu bifasha mu kwimakaza ihame ryo kudasiga inyuma abantu bafite ubumuga.

Ibi byatumye babona byinshi batari bafite mbere birimo kuba abagera 94% bafite ubumuga ubu bashobora kwivuza bakoresheje ubwisungane mu kwivuza (Mituweli), bikabafasha kubona insimburangingo n’inyunganirangingo mu buryo buboroheye, ibindi birimo kudahezwa mu mashuri no mu zindi nzego.

Imibare iheruka gutangazwa n'Ikigo cy'Igihugu cy'Ibarurishamibare (NISR), mu bushakashatsi ku isoko ry'umurimo bwo mu 2025, igaragaza ko 29.7% by'abafite ubumuga bari mu kigero cy'imyaka yo gukora mu Rwanda bari bafite akazi kabahemba cyangwa bakuramo inyungu.

MN202611_13lld34e9jy.t:
Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours , and issues for the National Security Agency (NSA). That's not to mention outages affecting the biggest US banks , as well as a major flaw found in a popular programming language .

These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked.

There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie.

As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.

A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.

It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.

Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.

Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.

But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.

AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.

And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.

Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.

Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.

"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.

In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.

This happened in the recent Java incident , as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.

These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.

Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.

A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.

With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.

Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.

In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.

"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."

In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.

At the same time, Anthropic, among other leading AI firms, has warned of the risks its own products pose .

Outages in particular have an impact on the physical world as they often cause disruption to healthcare, schools and people's ability to do their jobs.

Or, in the case over the weekend, planes' ability to fly.

Watch: Marco Rubio says recent tech outages are 'completely unrelated' to one another

They also shine a light on the world's heavy reliance on a small number of players.

Not just frontier AI companies, but infrastructure providers such as Microsoft and Amazon, which - along with Google - run a huge chunk of the world's computer servers.

In the PHP incident, the world was holding its breath as one programmer - working voluntarily - worked to issue patches in a form that was easily applicable.

And Java, run by another tech giant Oracle, is used by nearly all of the biggest companies on Earth.

"The Oracle Java vulnerability is a stark reminder of how dependent businesses have become on a relatively small number of critical technologies," said Sheila Pancholi, risk assurance lead at consultancy firm RSM UK.

"Organisations need to know where their critical technology dependencies sit, act quickly when vulnerabilities emerge, and test that their response has actually worked."

Meanwhile Xander Van Raemdonck, security engineer at Aikido Security, said the challenge was "knowing whether you're exposed".

"Java is bundled inside a huge amount of business software, so many companies don't have a full list of where it runs," he said.

The AI tools used to help find security flaws are still so new that they will probably continue to find vulnerabilities which have been lingering in code for decades.

"AI is accelerating discovery on both sides and speeding up how much software gets shipped," said Martin Reynolds, field CTO at software delivery company Harness.

"So the volume of what developers need to patch is going up, while the time they have to get the work done it is going down."

Tech debt will need to continue to be dealt with - which means more upgrades to systems and more potential for these to cause disruptions.

Plus there is the constant threat from hackers as they continue to get more sophisticated.

Attackers only need to find one vulnerability to exploit - whereas defenders have to protect against all potential hacks.

"Attackers can move quickly and carefree, and experiment without risk of failure so they can naturally often move a fraction faster," Helme said.

"We're currently observing that small delay between how fast the attackers can move and how fast the defenders can move."

The cat-and-mouse nature of the cyber-security game means it's unlikely to end any time soon - and the impact of AI means the stakes are getting higher.

MN202611_u6z58us1po.t:
Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.

Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.

But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.

That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.

Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.

How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.

The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.

The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation , external , as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.

While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.

It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.

There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.

Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.

The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.

But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.

Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come.

To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure.

The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down.

The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention.

As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay.

That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances.

Heimir Hallgrimsson celebrates the victory over Kosovo with Harvey Vale

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson says the controversy surrounding the Nations League games against Israel has made "this group stronger".

The players took a vote on whether to play the two matches - in September and October - amid protests over the Israel-Gaza war , with goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu making himself unavailable for selection.

The Republic of Ireland won the first match 3-0 in Hungary before a 1-1 draw in Serbia.

Hallgrimsson was speaking after his side defeated 10-man Kosovo 3-0 in Dublin on Tuesday night to finish runners-up to Austria in Group B3.

The second place means the Republic of Ireland will be in pot two for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw next month and also ensures they have a promotion/relegation play-off in March against a League A team as they try to move up to the top tier for the first time.

"It tested everyone - physically, mentally and no I've learned a lot doubt and the players have learned a lot and grown," said Hallgrimsson.

"I am pretty sure in one year, two years when this team becomes successful we will look back and say that was the defining moment for us.

"I am pretty sure we will look back in hindsight and say this was a huge moment for us.

"Us as leaders sometimes artificially create us against the world to get the group to stick together and I have said we have got that environment for free for two or three weeks and we survived it and it made this team and this group stronger."

Troy Parrott scored two penalties and Jack Moylan also netted against a Kosovo team hit by the dismissal of Kreshnik Hajrizi after 26 minutes.

It brought to an end a campaign which saw the Republic of Ireland win two matches, with two drawn and two lost.

"We know we will never be perfect and we are trying to find a way to win with what we have," Hallgrimsson added.

"I think we are getting better and better on that. Like I said in the first meeting when I was here and was introduced, I said I want to build a team that is difficult to play against and I feel like we are getting closer and closer to that.

"We are now consistent in our selection of players. We've more or less found our squad, our group and with doing that on a consistent basis, playing the same players together, playing the same system, the connections between players are starting to emerge."

The promotion/relegation play-off draw take place on Friday with the Republic set to go up against one of Croatia, Serbia, Denmark or Wales.

"Everybody, and especially us, like to play the top teams. For one, to compare yourself with the best teams, that's one thing," he said.

"Second, those teams will expose your weaknesses and that helps you in your growth to play these teams and they will expose your weaknesses so we can continue our growth. We're already looking forward to March.

"[There are] exciting teams in the pot. Whoever we draw, it's going to be two tough games and it's good for this team at this time to play these matches instead of friendlies, for example.

"So we're really excited for March and looking forward to meeting the players again."

Ivan Toney's trial will take place during the Euro 2028 tournament

A bid to move the date of England striker Ivan Toney's assault trial to avoid a clash with Euro 2028 has been refused.

The 30-year-old footballer, from Northampton, is accused of headbutting and punching Saber Da Silva during a confrontation at a nightclub in Wardour Street, central London, on 6 December.

Toney denied assault occasioning actual bodily harm at a court hearing last month and a date for a trial of up to four days was fixed for 12 June 2028, which is three days into the Uefa Euro 2028 tournament.

He represented England at this summer's World Cup and has made 10 international appearances. It is not yet known if he will be selected for Euro 2028, but the application was made in case.

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, where Toney did not appear, his barrister Mozammel Hossain KC said: "It came to our attention that… there may be potentially a football match called the European Championship in 2028 between 9 June and 9 July."

Hossain proposed a trial date in August that year, adding: "We ask you please that the matter be put back to then for a trial so that if the defendant is included in this football tournament he can play.

"My knowledge of football is very limited but I am told he was included in the last one in 2024 and the England squad for the World Cup."

Judge Tony Baumgartner called it a "speculative" application.

He refused the request, saying: "It does not seem to me to be in the interest of justice to disturb the date that was already fixed."

The judge said the application could be made again if Toney is selected for the England squad.

Toney missed out on the latest squad for the country's Nations League ties.

Toney started his football career with Northampton Town and played for teams including Wigan Athletic and Peterborough United before signing for Brentford in 2020.

He scored 72 goals during four years with the Bees before making a surprise switch in 2024 to Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli.

Watch: BBC correspondents discuss historic Trump, Xi and Putin meeting

Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in over a year on Wednesday, as the pair prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.

After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.

Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the conflict in Ukraine could be discussed.

However the main focus during the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.

After a warm reception from Xi, the leaders of the US and Russia shook hands ahead of a reception

It was not clear on Wednesday what form separate Trump-Putin talks would take, though a Kremlin spokesperson indicated short informal talks may happen without large delegations in the room.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.

Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough.

Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special".

In Shenzhen, a red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.

Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".

Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.

A lavish welcome ceremony was laid on for Trump's arrival

The south-east Chinese city the Apec summit is being held in is a booming area for manufacturing and advanced tech.

It comes against the backdrop of the ousting of Nvidia chief executing Jensen Huang, who admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of spying for Beijing - a claim dismissed as a "smear" by China.

Trump has pursued warmer relations with China but the incident points to ongoing tensions between the two powers.

Several hours before Trump's arrival, Putin landed in Shenzhen and held around two hours of talks with Xi, with whom he has pressed for closer economic and defence relations.

Xi said both countries would "move forward steadily and boldly" and that the relationship was "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".

The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner

The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.

Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.

You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.

The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford 's Igor Thiago.

In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.

It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton 's James Tarkowski.

Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.

Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United 's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.

And Liverpool argued against a late Crystal Palace penalty.

But which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.

Incident 1: Coventry 's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton 's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened."

Incident 2: Arsenal 's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City 's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence."

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry

When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.

The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.

The second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has said, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.

Incident 1: Thierno Barry put Everton in front against Coventry in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "On the balance of probability the ball did accidentally strike Barry's hand. However, the readily available footage did not provide conclusive evidence."

Incident 2: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty against Liverpool three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio. But was it just a clash of heads?

KMI Panel vote: 0:5 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "A penalty was incorrect with the contact being inevitable. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 3: Ipswich were awarded a 72nd-minute penalty against Bournemouth for a foul by Lewis Cook on Abdoul Ouattara.

KMI Panel vote: 1:4 incorrect on the field, but 4:1 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Ouattara made a clear step across Cook who didn't make a challenge and the referee's decision to award a penalty was incorrect. However, it was not a clear and obvious error."

Incident 4: Potential second yellow card for Bournemouth 's Marcus Tavernier.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field; no VAR intervention possible.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was a clear, deliberate action by Tavernier to delay the restart."

Some of the most high-profile decisions from across the weekend have not yet featured.

That is because they have been voted to be correct on the field and through VAR.

Incident 1: Leeds United 's Jayden Bogle caught Tottenham 's Mathys Tel on high on his ankle. There was no VAR review for a red card.

KMI Panel vote: 3:2 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "The majority felt Bogle was looking to challenge with his right leg and his left leg came down on the back of Tel's ankle without the speed, force or intensity to be serious foul play. Two panellists felt that the challenge was sufficiently dangerous to merit a red card."

Incident 2: Chelsea 's Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge by Sunderland 's Luke O'Nien.

KMI Panel vote: 4:1 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Clear contact made by O'Nien on Palmer which the panel felt should have been penalised with a free-kick on the basis that contact was made outside the area. One panellist felt that the foul contact was inside the area."

Incident 3: Sunderland were awarded a penalty when Levi Colwill was ruled to have tripped Brian Bobbey.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was upper body holding from both players as they progressed into the penalty area before a careless trip by the Chelsea defender."

Incident 4: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Lammens turned away from the ball, the contact he made on Suzuki was not impactful."

The KMI Panel was scrapped this summer in the Scottish Premiership because clubs became frustrated with the voting patterns of its members.

But it is more important in the Premier League, with the results creating a merit table which contributes to 50% of referees' salaries in bonus payments.

Many fans will feel there should have been more than two VAR errors logged in the last round of games.

Yet the KMI Panel does not exist to mirror the opinion of supporters.

Crucially, it uses the laws of the game and how the Premier League expects its games to be refereed as the barometer.

Still, six on-field mistakes - plus the Thiago red card - is clearly a high number.

And fans struggle to understand why it seems to be OK to have these on-field errors, and not correct them due to the high bar.

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith were banned for their part in the sandpaper plot

Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.

In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian, , external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.

"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."

For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.

Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".

On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.

"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."

Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.

Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.

In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:

Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before Bancroft was caught

Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"

Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper

When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"

Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".

Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.

Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.

The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.

Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.

A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."

A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.

"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.

"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."

In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.

"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.

"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.

"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.

"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."

'No way in a million years' the whole team didn't know - Vaughan on sandpaper scandal

Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.

The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.

"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.

"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.

"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.

"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.

"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."

Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.

In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb.

"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.

"He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".

"If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."

In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".

In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place.

"Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft.

"I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."

For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.

But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.

Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.

His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.

In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.

Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.

It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.

But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.

Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.

What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?

Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.

Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.

Prendergast made the tackle under investigation after Peceli Yato broke past him around the fringe of a ruck

Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast has been cleared to play in Saturday's Nations Championship match against South Africa after a panel ruled his hip-drop tackle against Fiji was not worthy of a red card.

The 23-year-old was not punished on the pitch after he wrapped his body around the back of Fiji flanker Peceli Yato's legs in a first-half tackle.

Hip-drop tackles, when a tackling player drops their hips and bodyweight on to the ball-carrier's legs, were outlawed by World Rugby before November's internationals.

A citing commissioner, who reviews match action and recommends retrospective punishment if they believe any incident merits a red card, highlighted Prendergast's tackle.

But Ireland successfully argued that the incident did not meet the threshold for a red card, clearing their first-choice fly-half for the weekend's meeting.

Prendergast's case was under scrutiny after South Africa coach Rassie Erasmus predicted he would escape punishment on a "technicality".

"We are in the northern hemisphere. I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play," said Erasmus on Monday, adding that he thought Prendergast's tackle was "terrible".

In the same Dublin media conference, Erasmus claimed France had got away with 17 hip-drops or knee-drops (where a player tackles an opponent while having a knee on the floor) in the Springboks' 21-19 loss in Paris last Friday.

Erasmus targeted the television match official Matteo Liperini for criticism.

"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.

Erasmus was banned for six Tests for his comments, with World Rugby saying his words constituted "an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials".

TMOs have been guided to only interrupt matches in cases of clear and obvious foul play as part of protocols agreed with head coaches, including Erasmus.

Erasmus' long list of grievances also includes Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong avoiding punishment for an alleged groin grab. South Africa front row Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban for a similar offence last year.

The 54-year-old has a history of criticising officials in public, having been banned for leaking an hour-long video pulling apart referee Nic Berry's performance in his team's first-Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions in 2021.

The following year, following a defeat by France, he posted a string of videos on social media questioning Wayne Barnes' decisions.

Both Berry and Barnes have spoken about the abuse they have received in the aftermath of Erasmus' criticisms.

By the time the music began at Wat Botum Park, Phnom Penh had already started to feel like one enormous family celebration. Cambodian dancers moved gracefully across the stage, Rwanda’s National Ballet answered with the energy of home, food stalls filled the warm evening air with competing aromas, and visitors wandered between colourful national pavilions as though the Francophone world had agreed, for once, to gather without quarrelling. But a few kilometres away, behind polished doors and guarded corridors, presidents, ministers and advisers were preparing for a political fight that would consume the summit. Outside, the drums kept a steady rhythm; inside, nobody could agree on who should hold the conductor’s baton.

President Paul Kagame and First Lady Jeannette Kagame had arrived in Cambodia on November 12 for a state visit and the 20th Francophonie Summit. They had come with a senior Rwandan delegation, a clear diplomatic programme and, as events later showed, no intention of being pushed quietly into a corner.

King Norodom Sihamoni received them at the Royal Palace, where the official welcome was followed by a private royal audience. Kagame and the First Lady also laid wreaths at Cambodia’s Independence Monument and at the memorial to the late King-Father Norodom Sihanouk. The gesture carried particular meaning; Rwanda and Cambodia were two countries marked by genocide, loss and reconstruction, and Kagame praised Cambodia for rebuilding itself after the Khmer Rouge period.

The Rwandan President then met the country’s most powerful political figures; Senate President Hun Sen, National Assembly President Khuon Sudary and Prime Minister Hun Manet. The programme moved from palace ceremony to political discussions, then to the Peace Palace, where Kagame and Hun Manet witnessed the signing of three agreements covering investment promotion, tourism and air services.

The two governments discussed Rwanda as a possible gateway for Cambodian products entering African markets, while Cambodia could offer Rwandan businesses an entry point into Southeast Asia. No direct Kigali–Phnom Penh flight was announced, so travellers still had to respect their connecting flights and airport waiting lounges; nevertheless, an air services agreement created the legal groundwork from which future connections could grow.

That evening, King Sihamoni hosted a state banquet in honour of Kagame, Jeannette Kagame and the Rwandan delegation. Hun Sen, Hun Manet and Cambodia’s First Lady, Pich Chanmony, joined the royal dinner. The menu remained private, perhaps wisely; when politicians were already disagreeing over the leadership of the Francophonie, there was no need to begin another argument over who had received the larger portion.

The summit itself was surrounded by lunches, dinners and those brief encounters that often mattered more than the speeches. Kagame and Jeannette Kagame joined other leaders for a luncheon hosted by Louise Mushikiwabo after the opening ceremony. They later attended a dinner hosted by Hun Manet in honour of the visiting heads of state and government.

Kagame also met Faure Gnassingbé, President of Togo’s Council, before the summit and was photographed talking with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during a break. These were the small but useful moments of international diplomacy; two leaders standing aside from the main room, exchanging a few words while officials hovered nearby, pretending not to listen.

The First Lady, Jeannette Kagame, had her own programme. She joined the spouses of visiting leaders for an audience with Queen Mother Norodom Monineath Sihanouk at the Royal Palace. It was a quieter and more intimate encounter in a week otherwise dominated by convoys, security cordons, television cameras and negotiators carrying folders thick enough to frighten an ordinary citizen.

At the Francophonie Village, Rwanda’s cultural presence was difficult to miss. Its National Ballet performed alongside Cambodian artists during the opening ceremony and continued drawing crowds with traditional dances. The Cambodian programme included a blessing dance, while Rwanda brought the powerful movement, rhythm and ceremony of its own heritage. The dancers did in a few minutes what diplomats sometimes failed to achieve in several days; they connected people without first demanding a procedural agreement.

The Village occupied about 10,000 square metres in the Wat Botum gardens and featured national pavilions, exhibitions, cultural performances and a gastronomy section. Around 100,000 visitors were expected during its five days. Rwanda’s stand promoted the country’s culture and tourism, while the dancers gave curious visitors a louder and more memorable invitation.

The delegation also carried a practical financial project. During the Black Swan Summit, Rwanda and Cambodia launched a pilot connecting Cambodia’s Bakong payment platform with Rwanda’s eKash system. The initiative was designed to make cross-border transfers faster and more affordable, with users eventually able to send money in their own currencies.

It was still a pilot, not a miracle button that could move money from Phnom Penh to Kigali before the waiter returned with the bill. But it showed preparedness; Rwanda had arrived with culture, diplomacy, investment agreements, aviation discussions and financial technology. It had not travelled across continents merely to occupy a chair in the family photograph.

At the centre of the storm was Louise Mushikiwabo, the Rwandan incumbent who had led the International Organisation of La Francophonie since 2018 and was seeking a third term. The Democratic Republic of Congo opposed her candidacy and threatened to leave the organisation if she were re-elected.

Kinshasa initially presented Juliana Amato Lumumba as its candidate, then offered to withdraw her and support former Romanian prime minister Dacian Cioloș as a supposed consensus candidate. Mauritania’s Coumba Bâ was also in the contest. What had been presented as an election was slowly becoming a complicated exercise in persuading Rwanda to remove itself from the race.

France’s President Emmanuel Macron reportedly wrote to Kagame and Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi, urging them to withdraw their candidates so that a compromise could be found. Rwanda refused.

Foreign Affairs Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe said plainly that Rwanda would not surrender its sovereign right to present a candidate simply because another country, powerful or otherwise, wanted it to withdraw. Rwanda also questioned how a Romanian could be declared Africa’s consensus candidate after an African state had withdrawn its own candidate to support him, despite an African Union decision urging African members of the Francophonie to rally behind one of the continent’s candidates. Snitches were lurking around, one political commentator present says.

Kigali’s argument was simple; if consensus failed, the organisation’s rules allowed a secret ballot decided by a majority. Rwanda wanted the members to vote. If Mushikiwabo had lost through the ballot box, the result would at least have emerged from the organisation’s agreed procedure. But those proclaiming that Rwanda was isolated appeared strangely reluctant to count the votes. Apparently, consensus was desirable; arithmetic was becoming dangerous.

The pressure then moved from formal letters into private rooms. French media reports described a heated meeting between Kagame and Macron, during which the Rwandan leader reportedly accused the French President of contributing to the division. Congolese officials rejected the suggestion that France had issued an order, insisting that Macron was only seeking a compromise. The exact words spoken behind closed doors were never published, but the room was evidently warmer than Phnom Penh’s weather required. Mushikiwabo’s selective wording, describing the French Presidency as outgoing sunk deep, at least from a French perspective.

Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye also became involved in efforts to break the impasse. Talks continued for hours, schedules slipped and delegates remained at the venue well beyond the expected closing time. The summit that had promised to reinvest in peace could not peacefully select its own secretary-general.

The final meeting brought more drama. Reports said Tshisekedi left before the official announcement, while his foreign minister, Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, was filmed appearing visibly upset and confronting a camera operator. The scene captured the mood; nobody had obtained precisely what they wanted, but everyone was already preparing to explain why the outcome proved they had won.

In the end, the leaders did not elect a new secretary-general and did not hold the vote Rwanda had requested. Instead, they extended Mushikiwabo’s mandate for another year and postponed the election while the organisation reconsidered its selection procedures. According to reports, the Cambodian proposal was supported by 37 members.

Rwanda had not secured the full third term it wanted, but neither had it withdrawn its candidate or accepted the immediate installation of the preferred alternative. Mushikiwabo remained in office, now entrusted with leading the organisation through the transition and proposed reforms. Rwanda had faced pressure from Kinshasa, Paris and other delegations; yet the meeting ended with the Rwandan incumbent still occupying the office.

The precise meaning of the agreement soon became another dispute. Congolese officials claimed Rwanda would be excluded from presenting a candidate in the next election. Nduhungirehe challenged that interpretation, accusing Kinshasa of circulating a misleading account of the summit’s decision. Even after everyone had gone home, the argument refused to pack its suitcase.

There was also an uncomfortable Romanian shadow over the effort to present Cioloș as the candidate who would unify the organisation. In January 2025, nearly 300 foreign military contractors hired by the Congolese government surrendered after M23 captured Goma. More than 280 of them were Romanian. They were disarmed, processed through Rwanda and transported to Kigali International Airport for their journey home.

Some had reportedly earned thousands of dollars each month while ordinary Congolese soldiers received a fraction of those amounts. Their adventure ended not with the triumph they had probably imagined, but with luggage inspections, buses through Rwanda and a silent departure from Kigali. It was an awkward history to remember while a Romanian politician was being promoted by Kinshasa as the answer to the Francophonie’s African leadership dispute.

There was no evidence connecting Cioloș personally to those contractors, but political symbolism rarely waited for such introductions. Romanian mercenaries had entered Congo carrying weapons and left through Rwanda carrying their bags; less than two years later, Kinshasa was asking African countries to abandon African candidates and support a Romanian for the Francophonie’s highest office. History had developed a peculiar sense of humour.

The timing sharpened the irony. On November 13, while Rwanda’s delegation was active in Cambodia, Rwanda supported a draft resolution in the United Nations General Assembly’s Third Committee opposing the use of mercenaries to violate human rights and obstruct peoples’ right to self-determination. The text passed at committee stage with 117 votes in favour, 54 against and seven abstentions. It still required the wider General Assembly process, but Rwanda’s position was clear; international principles should be applied consistently, regardless of the country or actors involved.

Phnom Penh therefore became much more than a dispute over Mushikiwabo. It was a display of how Rwanda had learned to clinically operate internationally; arriving prepared, using every part of a visit, placing culture beside commerce, building relationships beyond its traditional partners and refusing to mistake the influence of larger countries for authority over its sovereign decisions.

Rwanda was a geographically small country confronting a coalition of pressure far larger than itself. Yet it entered the royal palace with dignity, negotiated at the Peace Palace, displayed its culture at Wat Botum, connected its payment system to Asia, signed agreements, held strategic meetings and defended its position until the final session.

That resolve did not mean Rwanda had won everything. Mushikiwabo had not received a new four-year mandate, the election had been postponed, and the rules governing the next contest remained disputed. But Rwanda had refused to disappear simply because powerful actors considered its presence inconvenient. The summit had been forced to negotiate around Kigali’s position rather than over its head.

The conflict in eastern DRC remained the uninvited guest at every table. Kinshasa, accused Rwanda of supporting M23; Kigali denied backing armed groups and argued that its security concerns, including the presence of the FDLR and Congo’s use of foreign mercenaries, were repeatedly ignored.

Those competing claims were not resolved in Cambodia, and the suffering in eastern Congo remains far more serious than the quarrel over an international office.

Still, Phnom Penh told an important story about Rwanda’s global stature. The country had not presented itself as a passive guest waiting to be told where to sit. Its delegation had arrived with several missions and pursued them together; diplomacy, business, technology, culture and the defence of national sovereignty.

Outside the conference rooms, Rwanda’s dancers kept their rhythm and drew crowds.

Inside, Kagame and his delegation held their line while larger states searched for a compromise. Rwanda did not leave with everything it had sought, but it remained standing, its candidate remained in office, and its partnerships had expanded.

The politicians had spent days debating who should lead the orchestra; Rwanda’s dancers, meanwhile, had already shown everyone how to keep the beat. Iwacu tubyita “bangs tugendana”. And for Mushikiwabo, “on est ensemble”.

MN202611_e7ch4b5dl5.t:
Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei

In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.

If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.

Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.

But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.

Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.

He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.

The Canadian left Toronto University early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

Kuwait condemned the attack, which Iran said targeted an airbase hosting US forces (file photo)

Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.

The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.

It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.

The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.

The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.

Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump

Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington

Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack

On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.

The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".

"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.

Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".

The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.

Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".

The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.

Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.

"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.

On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.

Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.

In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.

Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".

At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

MN202611_hu2dvyvacs.t:
Nearly five years after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine turned him into a pariah, Putin is back on the global stage

But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.

Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.

Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.

That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.

It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.

"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.

That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.

But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.

It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.

One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.

In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."

But what of those who are not at the table?

Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.

Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.

Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.

It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".

In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.

Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.

Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.

It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.

The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.

It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.
